Not a single person stood up for me. Only the housemaid quietly stepped forward, straightened my blanket, and whispered, "No matter what happens, you still deserve kindness." In that moment, I finally understood who truly belonged in my life.**

The first time Vanessa called me worthless, people laughed.

The second time, I stopped caring.

If they wanted a performance, I was willing to give them one.

I remained seated in the middle of my family's magnificent ballroom, a gray blanket covering my legs while my hands rested motionless on the wheelchair's armrests. Crystal chandeliers reflected across polished marble floors as champagne flowed freely and conversations filled the room.

Everyone believed they had gathered to celebrate my return after the tragic accident that had supposedly left me permanently paralyzed.

Only one person knew the truth.

Me.

There was nothing wrong with my legs.

The collision had happened.

The wrecked car was real.

But the injury everyone believed in had never existed.

Only my doctors, my attorney, and the head of my security team knew I could stand up whenever I wanted. Everyone else believed I would never walk again.

Exactly as I intended.

Especially Vanessa.

She crossed the ballroom wearing a shimmering silver gown, the engagement ring I had once proudly placed on her finger sparkling beneath the lights. It no longer looked like a promise of love.

It looked like a prize she intended to keep.

Behind her stood my relatives, business associates, and several opportunists who had always stayed close to wealth rather than loyalty. Their expressions revealed curiosity more than concern.

Vanessa stopped directly in front of me.

She leaned closer until I could smell the wine on her breath.

"Look at you," she whispered with a cruel smile. "You're completely useless now. Who would ever want a man like this?"

Several guests shifted uncomfortably.

Not one of them spoke.

My uncle Martin pretended to study the floor.

Daniel, the man I had trusted for years, lowered his eyes without saying a word.

Vanessa's mother, however, seemed almost pleased.

I showed no emotion.

Vanessa casually flicked the blanket covering my legs with one perfectly manicured finger.

"I was supposed to marry someone powerful," she said. "Not someone who'll spend the rest of his life depending on everyone else."

I looked up at her calmly.

"We're still engaged."

She laughed as though I had made a joke.

"For now," she replied. "Let's see how long that lasts once your board realizes their CEO can't even enter a meeting without help."

That single sentence confirmed everything I needed to know.

She wasn't mourning what had happened to me.

She was waiting for me to lose everything.

Just then, someone quietly knelt beside my chair.

It was Clara.

The young housemaid who had worked in our home for the past three years.

Without saying a word, she gently pulled the blanket back into place after Vanessa had disturbed it.

Then she spoke so softly only I could hear.

"You still deserve to be treated with dignity."

Her words were barely louder than a whisper.

Yet they echoed through my mind louder than every conversation in that ballroom.

Vanessa rolled her eyes.

"How sweet," she mocked. "Looks like the maid is the only one who feels sorry for him."

Clara lowered her gaze.

But she refused to step away.

I looked down at her hand resting carefully on the blanket.

Steady.

Gentle.

Sincere.

Suddenly, memories flooded back.

Every time she had quietly brought me medication before I even asked.

Every moment she had spoken to me with genuine respect instead of pity.

Every silent glance she had given Vanessa whenever another cruel remark was made.

And for the first time, everything became perfectly clear.

The accident hadn't destroyed my life.

It had simply exposed the true character of everyone around me.
